You've heard what CDC and state public health programs are doing in using genomics in cancer control and prevention. Cancer has been the leading application for public health genomics. But genomics truly applies to all human diseases and affects all areas of public health. Almost two decades ago, CDC realized the profound opportunities and challenges for genomics in public health and created the CDC Office of Public Health Genomics. The office has been working with CDC programs, state public health, and other partners to effectively and responsibly translate genome discoveries into disease prevention and population health. We have three main strategies: Identify evidence-based genomic applications; inform and communicate with providers, policy makers, and the public; and integrate these applications into clinical practice and public health programs. A crucial function of public health genomics is to identify health impact in a rapidly emerging landscape of science and technology, specifically identifying which genomic applications and family history that are supported by synthesized evidence for their use; estimate the potential population health's impact, which can be measured in terms of lives saved, disease prevented, and healthcare cost savings; and finally, promoting appropriate and equitable use. This public health assessment function is needed more than ever as we continue to see amazing growth in the number of available genetic tests in the past two decades. As of March 30th this year, there are over 78,000 genetic tests for more than 4,000 diseases available through clinical research and practice. Almost 700 labs and more than 1,000 clinics are offering genetic testing for many diseases and conditions. What should be the appropriate public health response? To identify genomic tests and applications that are ready to impact health now, CDC has developed a simple classification schema for genomic tests based on rapidly changing levels of evidence. Tier one or green are ready applications that can be implemented today in practice. And you've heard two prominent examples today. Here are the three: Breast and ovarian cancer and Lynch syndrome. But there are also other things like newborn screening, which has been a prominent public health genetics program for more than 50 years. Tier two or yellow are applications for which there is insufficient evidence to support routine implementation, but they can provide information for informed decision-making on a case-by-case basis. In category includes, for example, many of the 200 pharmacogenomic tests that are on the FDA gene drug label. These tests are used for the prediction of patients' response to certain medications. Tier three or red are applications and tests that are not ready for routine implementation because they either lack evidence or there is evidence to recommend against their use. An example of tier three are direct to consumer personal genomic tests. Summarized today there are more than 40 tier one tests classified today; most of them are cancer-related. Their intended uses vary from diagnosis, prognosis, risk prediction, treatment, risk assessment, and pharmacogenomics. In fact, genomic applications today in tier one could benefit millions of people. Other than newborn screening, which affects all births, the two conditions discussed today are estimated to affect more than 1 million people in the United States. And most of them do not know they have these conditions. This calls for an important role for public health in saving lives and preventing disease. You heard about the one low-tech genomic application or two that's ready for use in public health today -- that's family health history. We know that family health history is a risk factor for many diseases. Use of family history offers opportunities for targeted screening and evidence-based interventions that can save lives and reduce the burden of many chronic disease in addition to cancer, diabetes, and heart disease, for example. Public health approaches to use family history are already in place. For over a decade CDC has been part of the Surgeon General Family Health History Initiative, which has developed an online free family health history tool available in four languages to encourage all Americans to collect family history information, especially around holidays when families gather. Thanksgiving Day has been declared by the Surgeon General the National Family Health History Day since 2004. So where are we now with genomics and public health and what does the future hold? The possibilities for genomics to improve public health are growing rapidly. More than a decade after the completion of the Human Genome Project, genome sequencing is cheaper and more reliable than ever. Whole genome sequencing has emerged as a powerful tool in both clinical and public health. Human DNA sequencing is increasingly used for the diagnosis of rare disease and tumor sequencing. Pathogen DNA sequencing has become an essential public health tool. The recently launched CDC Advanced Molecular Detection Initiative uses genomic technologies, and bar informatics, and surveillance, and outbreak control and detection. We've also seen increased public awareness and use of genetic tests, such as the increase in BRCA testing that followed Angelina Jolie's announcement about her own status and prophylactic surgeries. Last but not least, we are seeing a rapid proliferation of direct to consumer genetic tests by the private sectors. A million or more people have already sought such services in a changing paradigm of how genetic testing can be done. Supportives of direct to consumer testing praise it for allowing consumer empowerment; others have expressed concern that such testing does not adhere to evidence-based applications and best practices, and certainly, the use of genetic counseling before testing. Increasingly, a public health approach is needed to address challenges in genomic implementation across many diseases. You've heard about education of the public and healthcare community addressing healthcare systems limitations, such as collecting family health history and approaches to inform affected patients' relatives of their risks; promoting evidence-based policy and practice to support the appropriate use of genomic tests and reducing healthcare costs; collecting, analyzing population-level data on implementation and outcomes and assuring the lab quality of such testing; and last but not least, addressing health disparities to ensure benefits for all. The potential for widening health disparities in the genomics era is real. This is just one example of a study that illustrates disparities in BRCA testing by racial ethnic groups. This is a study of early onset breast cancer cases in young women from a national sample of about 14 million commercially insured patients. You can see that black and Hispanic women are significantly less likely to have BRCA testing compared to white women. Not only do these women miss out on the benefits of testing in terms of their own management, but their family members also miss out on the chance to find out if they're at risk. These types of data should be looked at across all genetic test and disease conditions, and reasons for disparities explored and addressed. Genomics is also increasingly addressed in national policy and legislation, including the Affordable Care Act, which now covers some evidence-based genomic services, such as BRCA, in accordance with the US Preventive Services Task Force recommendation, as well as newborn screening. The Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act or GINA prohibits discrimination and has coverage on employment based on genetic information. The inclusion of specific CPT codes for many genetic tests now allows us to track implementation and outcomes of genetic testing in the United States. And last but not least, HHS Healthy People 2020 objectives have added two new genomic objectives: Hereditary breast and ovarian cancer and Lynch syndrome. To summarize, you've seen this slide before in the context of cancer genomics but truly applies to all areas of genomic activities in public health across numerous disease programs. This includes surveillance, epidemiology and research, communication and partnerships, and public health practice. Finally, I'd like to end with a unique emerging opportunity for public health. In 2015, President Obama launched the US Precision Medicine Initiative. This initiative promises a new era of targeted treatment and prevention across many human diseases. The initiative has two components: Development of new cancer molecularly-targeted therapies and a national cohort of a million or more people which seeks to prospectively study genetic and nongenetic factors in health disease and other outcomes on a very large scale and also to use this information in developing new therapies and preventive interventions. How is this initiative relevant to public health? The success of the Precision Medicine Initiative requires a strong public health partnership to help ensure inclusion and generalizability and to focus on prevention, not just treatment. Public health is also needed to ensure an appropriate balance between long-term knowledge generation and immediate health gains within the cohort that are possible by implementing existing evidence-based genomic applications, such as the ones discussed today and others from the tier one CDC list. In the future we can look forward to a new era of precision public health in which health interventions can be targeted to population subgroups based on genetics and other factors, to maximize benefits of prevention strategies, minimize harms, and reduce healthcare costs of the 21st century. Thank you for your attention. [ Applause ] >> Okay. We have time for a few questions. I want to thank all the presenters. Cathy? >> From our online audiences, would the panel please address the perception that people may have that if they don't have the genes for a particular cancer, they are safe. That really needs to be accounted for. >> Muin, do you want to start with that? >> You've seen the slides, actually the slides have the risk of breast and ovarian cancer and colorectal cancer among people with or without carriage of these types of mutations. And if you are negative or BRCA1 or 2 or Lynch syndrome, you still don't have a background risk of breast, ovarian, and colorectal cancer. That depends on other risk factors, depends on your age, depends on other considerations. There may be other genes that haven't been measured yet. >> Dr. Jaffe? >> I know that the direct consumer marketing of these genetic tests is rated I guess as tier three, but presumably people are getting these tests; are they turning up to genetic counselors holding their test results and saying "Am I going to get breast cancer?" >> Deb, you want to take that? >> Yes, that's correct. So you are exactly correct, that that is happening in the genetics clinics, as well as in the primary care provider clinics as well, that people are bringing those test results, very confused about what they mean. And then also the providers need to try to figure out what's going on with that. Interestingly enough in Michigan, we're one of the very few states in the United States that we have a law that's been in place since 2000 that requires written informed consent to be obtained by a provider before any presymptomatic or predictive genetic test. But it would only apply to things that happen in Michigan. So it's certainly when we've looked at data from our behavioral risk factor surveys and compared it to other states, Michigan, we do seem to have way less awareness of that. And it may be somewhat related to that law compared to other states. So we're perhaps not seeing it as much in Michigan compared to other states, but we are definitely seeing it. >> Just to add to what Deb just said, a recent study of 1,000 customers who had these services, and within six months about a third of them took to their providers. And many of them emerged back from the provider interaction dissatisfied or unhappy of that interaction because the providers didn't know what to do with the information. So it's a confusing market out there. There are other reasons why people do DTC testing, like ancestry and, you know, recreation. I mean, they have fun, they like to do other things. But for health-related purposes, we call them tier three. >> So Lindsay, did you want to say anything as someone who's been tested? >> Yeah, I think this is a hard gamble. As somebody who, you know, is talking to women day in and day out about this information, and trying to get them over this really critical hurdle, there's so many people that should be getting tested that aren't. We need to make sure that we're doing this responsibly, that when people get the results, that there is a huge uptake in terms of doing something with those results. We very much believe -- we talk about this all the time at Bright Pink -- that it's not just about knowledge, it's not just about awareness; it's about what do you do as a result of that? And so I think having a really thoughtful partner in your provider, which is why, you know, the program Bright Pink is going out and delivering in communities nationwide is so critical because we need to make sure that these providers are totally equipped to have this conversation to support the action that drives that as a result. >> We'll take a question from the online audience. >> So from our Grand Rounds email box, Dr. Richardson advocates genetic counseling for individuals who may have increased risk for cancer. Could Dr. Richardson or other speakers comment on one, the adequacy of the number of genetic counselors compared to the number of people who seek or need genetic counseling, and two, national efforts to increase the number of genetic counselors? >> So we all heard that story on NPR yesterday. And we thought it was quite timely for today's presentation. This is a shortage of genetics counselors who are board certified, and Deb can speak to that. I think some of the things they're doing in Michigan that they're doing in other places is telephonic counseling. Telehealth is now becoming bigger and bigger so you can reach audiences or people in need who don't have counselors where they are. I am not aware -- and Deb may know more about what the training -- how training is being ramped up to have more counselors trained. >> So yes, you are correct. The American Board of Genetic Counselors, the National Society of Genetic Counselors have definitely been trying to think of ways to increase the number of genetic counselors. One of the issues is that the genetic counselors are moving from clinical practice into industry. And so to keep those genetic counselors in clinical practice new things are happening like increases in salary, which is a very good idea, but also programs are really trying to increase their capacity. For instance, I'm a Northwestern University graduate of their genetic counseling program. This year they had 13 graduates, but next year they're taking 20. >> The only other thing I will add is that I think it's just really important to make sure that we're thinking about where especially young women are in offering the information, how they're used to receiving content. And I think part of our efforts to create a digital one-stop-shop so to say that really demystifies this process, I think. Because we do know sometimes when people are referred to genetic counselors, that middle step can actually be a hindrance in itself. So I think this is a really tricky evolving situation. Since Ashkenazi Jews are disproportionately affected or more likely to have BRCA genes, what is CDC doing, what are states likely to do, what do we support the states to do, and what avenues are you looking at? And I'll just name a few and then go away. So one is that Jewish women typically are very tightly bound to their parents even beyond marriage. And the mother commonly is in a sisterhood at her temple. So that's one thing. Another situation is there are colleges that are relatively high percentage Jewish women population. I'm told Emory is, like, one-third total men and women Jewish. So that's another target. And since we're talking about the proper targeting and communication, I wonder if we've started to make that attempt. So thank you, however you take it. >> Thanks, Rich. So to answer your question, we have been working with several Jewish groups, one in particular. So we have identified that as a population to which we reach out to specifically. I can't -- don't have time to go into all the details, but I'll be happy to talk with you later. But yeah, we have recognized that as a specific need. So I think that's all the questions that we can take now -- I'm sorry, one more? Okay. >> Again, from our Grand Rounds email box. This one's a little broad. What are your recommended strategies for public health organizations to provide education, screening, and referrals for BRCA1 and 2 testing? >> So Deb, that's right up your alley, I'll let you take it or start. >> I'm a huge advocate of epidemiology and data and starting there to really try and figure out where the needs are in your community and then to target your education efforts based on that. Otherwise I think it's going to become way too broad and not so focused. But one easy target is if your state does have a large Ashkenazi Jewish population, that would be a very easy place to start. So that would be my number one focus for people. But it does seem when we look at our data -- and I would encourage people to look at this -- is really look at the ovarian cancer cases because I think that is a very, very important group that definitely needs these services and that all ovarian cancer patients would greatly benefit for this. title: How to Prepare for Your Mammogram
description:
Regular mammograms are more than just a screening, they're a powerful tool in the fight against breast cancer. Early detection can save lives!

Time for your mammogram? Use these tips to prepare.
- Avoid having your mammogram while you’re on your period (or the week before it is due to come!) 
- On the day of your screening, skip deodorant, powders, or perfumes. These can stain the X-ray.
- You’re going to need to be undressed from the waist up, so plan accordingly! You may want to opt for a top and bottoms (like pants, shorts, or a skirt) rather than a dress.

description:
‼️New cancer science ‼️

A new blood test to detect cancer (plus new science on how it works)

The ctDNA test has actually been around for many years but new studies are showing it’s usefulness in breast cancer - especially triple negative.

Here’s how it works.

When cancer cells break down through their natural cell cycle, they release small pieces of genetic material into the blood stream. This is known as circulating tumor DNA.

With a simple blood draw, you can start to detect is tiny fragments of genetic material are present - meaning there is likely cancer somewhere in the body.

Now - what’s interesting is that these levels are starting to be used in triple negative breast cancer to determine likelihood of recurrence. If you have a positive test when you finish treatment, higher risk of recurrence.

But here is where the science is lacking😬

What do you do about a positive test?
‼️More frequent follow up?
‼️Treatment?

This is exactly what the ZEST trial is currently attempting to answer. More on that soon.

title: Breast biopsies are ordered when breast cancer may be present. More info in description! #Biopsy
description:
Breast biopsies are ordered when breast cancer may be present. During this process, the doctor removes small pieces of breast tissue from the suspicious area so they can be looked at in the lab to see if they contain cancer cells.

Rest assured, needing a breast biopsy does not necessarily mean you have cancer; in fact, most test results show no breast cancer present according to the American Cancer Society. 

Our team understands the anxieties and uncertainy that comes with a breast biopsy order. We are here to walk you through every step with compassion and expertise. #BreastBiopsy #BreastCancer #Awareness

transcript_text: [Music] How to find a doctor for a thorough clinical breast exam. If you're wondering how to find the right doctor for a detailed clinical breast exam, you're taking an important step toward breast health. A clinical breast exam is a physical checkup where a health care professional uses their hands to feel for any unusual lumps, thickening, or other changes in your breasts and underarm area. It's a key part of early detection and prevention, especially since guidelines recommend starting these exams around age 25 or earlier if you have increased risk factors. Start by looking into your health insurance network. Most insurance plans cover primary care doctors, gynecologists, internists, nurse practitioners, and physician assistants who are trained to perform these exams. If you don't have a regular doctor, consider reaching out to local hospitals or women's health clinics. Many clinics offer new patient appointments where you can meet a provider, discuss your health history, and get a thorough breast exam. These clinics often have dedicated women's health services, making it easier to find someone experienced in breast health. You can also ask trusted friends or family members for recommendations. They might suggest providers they trust or have had good experiences with. Another option is to contact local hospitals directly or visit community health centers, which often provide comprehensive breast health services. When choosing a provider, consider your comfort level. Some women prefer gynecologists because of their specialized training in women's health, but primary care physicians and nurse practitioners are also wellqualified to perform clinical breast exams. During your appointment, the health care provider will use their hands to carefully feel your breasts and underarm areas for any abnormalities. They may ask if you've noticed any changes or symptoms like lumps, pain, or skin changes. Remember, clinical breast exams are most effective when combined with other screening tools like mamogs, especially since exams alone can sometimes miss early signs of cancer. It's important to discuss with your provider how often you should have a clinical breast exam based on your personal risk factors. For most women at average risk, these exams are recommended every 1 to three years, starting at age 25. If you have a family history of breast cancer or other risk factors, your doctor might suggest more frequent exams or additional screening. In summary, finding a qualified doctor involves checking your insurance network, seeking recommendations, and reaching out to local clinics or hospitals. Schedule an appointment, share your health concerns, and ask about your screening plan. Regular clinical breast exams along with mamograms and breast awareness are vital tools in early detection and maintaining breast health. title: Mammography Screening Guidelines-Mayo Clinic
description: The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recently revised its screening recommendations for breast cancer based upon an analysis of various mammography screening schedules.  Experts suggest screening every two years for average risk women ages 50 to 74 achieves most of the benefits of annual screening, but with less harm. Furthermore, although there was a decrease in mortality for women ages 40 to 49, screening resulted in additional mammograms and false positives, therefore is not being recommended. These findings are published in the November 17, 2009 Annals of Internal Medicine. Sandhya Pruthi, M.D., director of Mayo Clinic Breast Clinic, Rochester, Minn., responds to this news.

title: Think Pink: How Your PCP Can Help Prevent Breast Cancer and More | Greater Tri Cities IPA
description:
October is Breast Cancer Awareness Month, and it’s more than just pink ribbons—it's your reminder to take charge of your health through preventive care with your Primary Care Physician (PCP).

Early detection saves lives. With a 99% survival rate when caught early, breast cancer screenings—along with checkups for other silent conditions like heart disease and diabetes—should be a top priority.

In this video, Greater Tri Cities IPA shares how building a relationship with a trusted PCP in North San Diego County can help you stay ahead of illness, reduce anxiety, and make empowered decisions about your health.

✅ Learn what screenings are recommended
✅ Discover how your PCP supports early detection
✅ Understand the emotional benefits of routine checkups
✅ Find out what’s included in your annual wellness visit

👉 Don’t wait—book your wellness visit today with a GTC physician and take control of your health journey.

🔗 Find a doctor near you: https://greatertricitiesipa.com/physicians/

🔗 Learn more: https://greatertricitiesipa.com

Blog content and video editing by Christina Zarate, HHP, MQP.

Christina is your trusted partner in holistic care and wellness. With over 25 years of experience and practice with clients in massage therapy and holistic health coaching, she specializes in a wide range of techniques through manual lymphatic drainage, Qigong, and Thai relaxation therapy that address health, pain relief, weight management, and overall wellness. Christina’s expertise extends beyond traditional massage therapy; she’s also a passionate advocate for the latest healthcare trends, nutrition, sleep optimization, biohacking, and fitness strategies.

title: Catastrophizing: How to Stop Making Yourself Depressed and Anxious: Cognitive Distortion Skill #6
description:
Learn how to stop catastrophizing, a cognitive distortion that fuels anxiety and depression. Discover practical strategies to manage catastrophic thinking.
Join Therapy in a Nutshell’s membership: https://courses.therapyinanutshell.com/membership
You'll get instant access to all 10 life-changing courses, live weekly Q&As, and a supportive community for just $27/month. Learn how to manage anxiety, process trauma, regulate emotions, and build lasting resilience so that you can live a deeply rich and meaningful life! 

In this video, we’re going to talk about catastrophizing- expecting the worst! Catastrophizing is an excellent way to make yourself anxious and depressed and completely ruin your life! Oh yeah, and I’m going to teach you 3 things you can do to stop catastrophizing.
What is Catastrophizing:
Catastrophizing is a common cognitive distortion, or thinking error. It’s when we think of a current or future situation as a catastrophe. So for example, you worry that you’re going to fail a test. Then you imagine what would happen when you do fail- you’re going to get kicked out of school, end up working a dead end job, fail at life at life and die homeless on the street. And all this because of a test at school. 

Catastrophizing is imagining the worst. It’s taking a difficult situation and interpreting it as being horrible, terrible, and unrecoverable. We’ve all known that person who, if they got a “B” on a test wailed “I’m failing Math class”.  Many of us have had that parent who, when we didn’t want to do our chores they said something like “If you don’t do your chores, your college roommates will hate you and no one will want to marry you.”

Like in the story about the jack, Catastrophizing often starts with a genuine setback, like getting a flat tire in the middle of nowhere, but then the thinking error turns that reality into the belief that something horrible is bound to happen- “I’m going to get shot, attacked and robbed!”. 

At its root, catastrophizing is about our habitual response to challenges or shortcomings. So take a second, pause this video and ask yourself: How do you think about failure? 

Catastrophizing is a thinking error (aka cognitive distortion) that makes you anxious, depressed, and unmotivated.

5. Remember, that quick pinch is helping to save someone’s life. And you’ll feel great knowing you have made a lifesaving difference.

Make an appointment today at RedCrossBlood.org.

title: 10/11 NOW: Bryan Health Patient Survives Colon Cancer Diagnosis with Early Screening & Support
description:
A Bryan Health patient is sharing her journey with colorectal cancer and the importance of preventative screenings and support after diagnosis. March is Colorectal Cancer Awareness Month. 

Tiffany Mullison is a foster care worker in Lincoln. In January 2024, she underwent her first colonoscopy at the age of 54. The results were abnormal. Shortly thereafter, Mullison had a colon resection procedure to eliminate the polyps. Thankfully, the cancer was caught at a very early stage. No additional treatment was required and follow-up colonoscopies have cleared her for the next two years.

After a cancer diagnosis, support is essential. Patients can work with oncology nurse navigators. Nurse navigators are specially trained nurses and social workers who help patients through each step of cancer care. They provide information, answer questions, coordinate appointments and give support.

Geschke specializes in gynecologic and gastrointestinal cancers. She provided support and guidance to Mullison after her initial diagnosis and throughout her treatment. Geschke was particularly helpful to Mullison by interpreting test results and recommending reputable websites and podcasts for personal research. 

Mullison is sharing her story to raise awareness for colon cancer during March. Admittedly, she didn’t realize the screening guidelines had changed to encourage earlier detection. Mullison also wants to decrease the stigma surrounding colon cancer, saying she struggled to tell people about her diagnosis because she felt embarrassed.

“There’s no pink ribbon for colon cancer,” she added. “People aren’t embarrassed to get a mammogram, why should they be ashamed to get a colonoscopy? Today, I’m talking with all my friends in their mid-50’s and encouraging them to get screened. I’m even driving them to their appointments!”

10/11 NOW reporter, Sam Cobb has the story!

title: Cancer survivors hope new test gets more people screened
description:
Sarah DeBord is a wife, mother and avid runner.

"I was probably the fittest I've ever been in my life. I was training for multiple races, working up to a half marathon," she said.

But three years ago, she started experiencing a variety of unpleasant symptoms.

"I blamed [the symptoms] on all the running I was doing," DeBord said. "So the exhaustion, the weight loss, blood in your stool and change in bowel habits, were four obvious things that I wrote off and excused for other things in my life."

A trip to the doctor led to a colonoscopy, and at the age of 34, she was diagnosed with colon cancer.

"I had two very small kids at home who I wondered, if I died of cancer, would they even be old enough to remember me?" DeBord said.

Fortunately, doctors were able to control her cancer with chemotherapy.

"So as of right now, I'm living with what they call chronic cancer, where I have the potential to live a nice, long life," DeBord said.

Meanwhile, officials from the Colon Cancer Coalition in Edina say they're strong advocates of colonoscopies. However, they say people don't always get screened when they should.

"Honestly, it's fear. Fear of the procedure, fear of the prep, fear of knowing," said Erin Peterson, communications director of the Colon Cancer Coalition.

Now, a new screening test exists called Cologuard, which allows people to test for colon cancer from their home by providing a stool sample and mailing out the box.

"We are very excited about anything that will get more people screened," Peterson said of Cologuard.

That said, if the Cologuard test comes up positive, people would still need a follow-up colonoscopy to confirm it.

"Some people probably find that embarrassing," DeBord said, referring to the colonoscopy.

While some people get embarrassed about the invasive nature of a colonoscopy, it helped save DeBord's life.

"I know that there's a long term forecast for my life, so that's definitely the difference for me," she said.

Cologuard is approved for use by men and women age 50 and older. The test has to be prescribed by a licensed provider and can't be purchased over the counter.

If you want to hear more about Sarah DeBord's battle with cancer, check out her blog.

description:

There are many embarrassing bodily functions that people often feel uncomfortable talking about so on this show, we look at bowel cancer and Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS).

Bowel cancer killed roughly fifteen thousand people in the UK last year. That makes it the second most lethal form of cancer in Britain. If caught early, bowel cancer is treated with a very high success rate. The issue is that people often wait too long to discuss they bowel issues with a Doctor, usually due to embarrassment. 

Problems with your bowels don’t always mean cancer. There are a multitude of other issues, including IBS.

Chrissy’s guests include Stephen Browne to talk about his experience with bowel cancer, ‘Beating Bowel Cancer’ representative, Graham Kelly to talk about the work the charity does and a bowel expert to discuss the common bowel problems and go into detail about what IBS is.

❓ QUESTIONS ANSWERED
Q: Is it normal to have a bowel movement three times a day or only three times a week?
A: Both are within the normal range. What matters more than frequency is your personal baseline and whether something changes. If a shift persists for more than three to four weeks, bring it to your doctor.

Q: Do I need a colonoscopy if I feel perfectly healthy?
A: Yes. Colorectal cancer often produces no symptoms until it has reached an advanced stage. Colonoscopy does not just detect cancer, it prevents it by finding and removing precancerous polyps before they become dangerous. Screening is recommended starting at age 45 for average-risk individuals.

Q: Can stress actually cause real digestive problems or is it all in my head?
A: It is in your anatomy, not your head. Stress activates the fight-or-flight nervous system response, which diverts blood flow from digestion, changes gut motility, increases acid production, and makes the gut lining more sensitive. The result is real physical symptoms including bloating, cramping, reflux, and irregular bowel habits.

title: Four Common Types of Shoulder Pain and Options for Treatment
description:
Shoulder pain can significantly impact a person's mobility, but not all pain is equal. Michael A. Vazquez, MD, discusses four different kinds of shoulder pain and the treatments available at Milford Regional Orthopedics & Sports Medicine.

transcript_text: Hello, I'm Dr. Michael Vasquez. I'm an orthopedic surgeon, sports medicine specialist here at Milford Regional Physician Group. Just here to talk to you for a few minutes about the most common causes of shoulder pain and problems that I see in my office. Number one on that list would be rotator cuff problems. And rotator cuff problems can run from a tear in the rotator cuff to simply inflammation around the rotator cuff. Both these problems can cause pain and these are common reasons why patients see me in the in my office. The treatment for rotator cuff problems do depend on the actual extent of the inflammation or the tearing. However, in general we think about bringing down the inflammation with medications such as non-steroidal anti-inflammatories, but also in my practice I will give patients cortisone injections to help with inflammation. And then there are times where patients require surgery to repair the rotator cuff. Typically, at least once a week, unfortunately, somebody needs that surgery to have their rotator cuff repaired. Another common cause of shoulder pain that I see in my office is arthritis. Arthritis can affect any joint in your body. In the shoulder, there are two joints. The main ball and socket joint, as well as the smaller AC joint that's on the top of the shoulder. Arthritis is when the cartilage wears down and inflammation occurs causing the pain. In my practice, when I see patients with arthritis in their shoulder, our main objective is to get them feeling better and to improve their function. So, typically this includes anti-inflammatory medications, physical therapy, and unfortunately, if patients are continuing to have severe pain, surgical options such as arthroscopic surgery or shoulder replacements can be very helpful at relieving the pain associated with arthritis in the shoulder. Another very common cause of shoulder pain that I see in my office is something called frozen shoulder. And it essentially is inflammation throughout the whole shoulder joint that freezes the shoulder where patients feel their motion is very limited and quite painful. This is a problem that can happen after an injury or even most often patients really don't know why it started. So, in my office, I typically do treat this with a steroid injection if the patient would like cuz that really does a great job at bringing down the inflammation and getting some pain relief. Also, physical therapy to help regain that motion that they've lost because of the problem. Most patients with frozen shoulder do not need surgery and will eventually improve over time in treatment. The last common cause that I I typically will see in my office is pain from that's actually referred from their necks, from the C spine, from the cervical spine. So, what that means are the nerves that come from your neck go down into your shoulder and down your arm. And there are patients that I will see in my office who have shoulder pain. However, the problem isn't actually with the shoulder joint itself and can be coming from pinched nerves from their cervical spine. So, whenever I examine patients with shoulder pain, I typically start with their uh neck range of motion to try to figure out if this is actually a pinched nerve as opposed to a primary shoulder problem. As a orthopedic sports medicine specialist, I do focus in on surgical treatment for many problems, but also non-surgical approaches as well. And in our new office here on Prospect Street, we have uh many other practitioners that as well specialize in both surgical and non-surgical options for not just shoulder pain, but essentially every other joint pain that that may occur. So, this would be a place where you could come to be evaluated and appropriately referred to the proper physician that can further treat you.

description:
Learn about the treatment options you have for localized Prostate Cancer. This video features Dr. John Lynch, Prostate Cancer Survivor and Chair of the Urology Care Foundation’s Public Education Council. Take control of your prostate cancer. The Urology Care Foundation is the official foundation of the American Urological Association. The Urology Care Foundation raises awareness of urologic health through national public health campaigns. More awareness helps reduce embarrassment and fear.  It also helps patients take an active role in their care. #ProstateCancer #ProstateHealth #UrologyCareFoundation

We support urologic research and strive to provide the most current, comprehensive and reliable urologic health information for patients and the public. The Foundation:
- Was founded in 1987.
- Supports research professionals through grant programs, clinical trials and the publishing of the National Urology Research Agenda (NURA).
_ Provides resources for patient education regarding urological conditions including brochures.
- Engages in public awareness campaigns, special events and community programs to help further the cause of educating those at risk and as those already suffering from urological conditions.
- Supports and advocates on a variety of issues pertaining to patient urological health, industry standards and access to care.
- Is supported by a wide variety of corporate sponsors, endowments and individual donors.
- Publishes Urology Health Extra magazine as a service to the patients, health care professionals and the public.

transcript_text: Millions of people around the world will be diagnosed with bulimia nervosa in their lifetime. If left untreated, bulimia nervosa can be a life-threatening condition. My name is Dr. Rachel Goldstein, and I am an adolescent medicine physician who specializes in taking care of teens and young adults. I've treated many patients who have struggled with bulimia nervosa, which I'll refer to as bulimia in this video. In the next few minutes, we'll go over what bulimia is, common behaviors and misconceptions associated with bulimia, and where you or your loved one can find support and treatment. To get a sense of what bulimia can look like, I'd like to tell you about Alice. Alice is a fictional example of a patient who represents many cases that I see every year. Alice is a 17-year-old girl who has been struggling with negative body image for the last year. Her parents noticed her eating late at night, and her weight going up over the last few months, but figured it was just due to stress around college applications. It wasn't until they found drawers full of candy wrappers and noticed she often spend over an hour in the bathroom after dinner, that they realized Alice might have bulimia. Bulimia is a type of eating disorder marked by episodes of bingeing followed by behaviors that attempt to compensate for the binge, as people often worry about their body shape or size. During binge episodes, people will eat a large amount of food, often entire bags of chips, boxes of cereal, or packages of sweets that might be upwards of a thousand calories over a relatively short amount of time. During these episodes, there's generally a feeling of being out of control and intense feelings of guilt and shame. Unlike binge eating disorder, however, these binge episodes will be followed by different behaviors that try to make up for {slash} compensate for the binge. These include things like vomiting, over exercise, diet pills, diuretics, or laxatives. People engage in these behaviors to try to avoid weight gain that often goes along with binge eating. For some, they may try to restrict their eating after a binge, leading to intense feelings of hunger, which may ultimately trigger another binge episode, and the cycle continues. To be officially diagnosed, these episodes need to happen at least once a week for at least 3 months. As a result of these cyclical eating patterns, people with bulimia are often within a healthy weight range or slightly overweight, but typically not underweight. The misconception that patients with eating disorders are all underweight can make it harder for patients struggling with bulimia to be diagnosed. Bulimia affects women more than men, and typically presents in their late teens and early 20s. From the outside, it may be hard to tell if someone has bulimia, because those struggling with eating disorders often attempt to engage in their bingeing and purging behaviors in secret. You may notice a loved one making negative body image comments, you may see food disappearing more quickly than expected, or find hidden food wrappers. You may notice your loved one avoid eating out or in a group, engaging in excessive exercise, or see them going to the bathroom immediately after meals. Sometimes, recurrent plumbing problems may be a tip-off that your loved one is engaging in self-induced vomiting. Disordered eating doesn't happen in a vacuum. Patients with bulimia nervosa often have a history of other psychiatric diagnoses, such as depression, anxiety, substance abuse, or post-traumatic stress disorder. Personality disorders can often occur in those with bulimia. Understanding that multiple mental health conditions can happen at the same time is important as addressing each one may be needed as part of treatment. Specifically, suicidality, which includes thoughts about hurting oneself as well as suicide attempts, happens more often in those with bulimia than in the general population. This is one of the many reasons why if either you or someone you care about is struggling with bulimia, it's important to get help. Often, it's the medical complications of bulimia that worry people most. Bingeing can cause abdominal discomfort and heartburn in the short term, and over time may lead to weight gain despite the compensatory behaviors. But usually, it's the behaviors like vomiting, laxatives, diuretics, and diet pills that can cause some of the more serious risks to one's health. Physically, people engaging in self-induced vomiting may notice teeth sensitivity, swelling of their parotid glands, which are found beneath the cheeks, or blood in their vomit, which is a sign of injury to the gastrointestinal tract. People may also notice rough patches or redness over the knuckles as a result of teeth rubbing over the back of the hand with self-induced vomiting. If a doctor orders blood work, they may see abnormally low electrolytes. Heart testing may show abnormal heart rhythms, and the combination of electrolyte and heart rhythm abnormalities can be life-threatening. The guilt and shame around bulimia can make it challenging for those struggling with this disorder to talk about it, which is the first and most important step in the recovery process. If you suspect a loved one has bulimia, it's important to approach them from a place that is judgment-free and as supportive as possible. Pick a time when neither of you are rushed or multitasking. You can start out by describing the specific behaviors you've observed that make you worried. For example, "I've noticed that you're often in the kitchen late at night and seem to be staying in the bathroom for a while after most meals. I've also heard you make negative comments about your body. I'm worried that you might have an eating disorder. Is this something that you're dealing with?" Ideally, your loved one is in a place where they can open up about their eating disorder, but this doesn't always happen. If your concerns are dismissed or rejected, it's important to let the person know that you care about them and are there to support them. If they're minor, it's important to connect them with a medical and mental health care provider for evaluation. Effective treatments involve a combination of psychotherapy, nutrition counseling, and medical care. The main treatment is psychotherapy, specifically cognitive behavioral therapy. Mental health providers can help patients identify and reframe negative thoughts about body image and work towards developing a healthier relationship with food. In adults, antidepressant medication can be effective as part of the treatment for bulimia. Partnering with a medical provider and dietitian can help address some of the potential medical consequences of bulimia and establish healthy eating and exercise habits. For most people, treatment will take place in the clinic setting, though a small number will benefit from higher levels of care, like day programs, and rarely inpatient hospitalization. For the friends and family of those struggling with an eating disorder, seeing the eating disorder as something separate from their loved one is key in the recovery process. I find it helpful to imagine a Venn diagram where we have the eating disorder and the patient. When the eating disorder is strong, these two circles can really overlap, but over time we work to split them apart, and it starts with viewing the eating disorder as its own thing. Most patients will have bulimia for at least 12 months, and more than half will recover. The longer someone has an eating disorder, the lower the chance of recovery. Over time, about 1/3 will have a recurrence of their eating disorder. Help is available for those who need it. Talking to your primary care provider can be a great place to start. As someone who struggle with bulimia may also have other mental health diagnoses, it's important to seek help immediately if there's ever any concern for safety, like thoughts of hopelessness or suicide. I've taken care of many patients who have struggled with disordered eating who were able to recover and develop a healthy relationship with food and their bodies. Alice, whose story we shared earlier, was one of those fortunate ones. She was reluctant to talk to her parents at first, but eventually was able to open up to them about her eating disorder. She worked with a therapist, a dietitian, and her doctor for 2 years, and continues to see a therapist now that she's in college. Acknowledging the eating disorder thoughts can feel overwhelming and is an important first step towards getting help and beginning the recovery process. To get help or additional resources, please check in with your primary care provider.

From the outside, it may be hard to tell if someone has bulimia, because those struggling with eating disorders often attempt to engage in their bingeing and purging behaviors in secret. You may notice a loved one making negative body image comments, you may see food disappearing more quickly than expected, or find hidden food wrappers. You may notice your loved one avoid eating out or in a group, engaging in excessive exercise, or see them going to the bathroom immediately after meals. Sometimes, recurrent plumbing problems may be a tip-off that your loved one is engaging in self-induced vomiting. Disordered eating doesn't happen in a vacuum. Patients with bulimia nervosa often have a history of other psychiatric diagnoses, such as depression, anxiety, substance abuse, or post-traumatic stress disorder. Personality disorders can often occur in those with bulimia. Understanding that multiple mental health conditions can happen at the same time is important as addressing each one may be needed as part of treatment. Specifically, suicidality, which includes thoughts about hurting oneself as well as suicide attempts, happens more often in those with bulimia than in the general population. This is one of the many reasons why if either you or someone you care about is struggling with bulimia, it's important to get help. Often, it's the medical complications of bulimia that worry people most. Bingeing can cause abdominal discomfort and heartburn in the short term, and over time may lead to weight gain despite the compensatory behaviors. But usually, it's the behaviors like vomiting, laxatives, diuretics, and diet pills that can cause some of the more serious risks to one's health. Physically, people engaging in self-induced vomiting may notice teeth sensitivity, swelling of their parotid glands, which are found beneath the cheeks, or blood in their vomit, which is a sign of injury to the gastrointestinal tract. People may also notice rough patches or redness over the knuckles as a result of teeth rubbing over the back of the hand with self-induced vomiting. If a doctor orders blood work, they may see abnormally low electrolytes. Heart testing may show abnormal heart rhythms, and the combination of electrolyte and heart rhythm abnormalities can be life-threatening. The guilt and shame around bulimia can make it challenging for those struggling with this disorder to talk about it, which is the first and most important step in the recovery process. If you suspect a loved one has bulimia, it's important to approach them from a place that is judgment-free and as supportive as possible. Pick a time when neither of you are rushed or multitasking. You can start out by describing the specific behaviors you've observed that make you worried. For example, "I've noticed that you're often in the kitchen late at night and seem to be staying in the bathroom for a while after most meals. I've also heard you make negative comments about your body. I'm worried that you might have an eating disorder. Is this something that you're dealing with?" Ideally, your loved one is in a place where they can open up about their eating disorder, but this doesn't always happen. If your concerns are dismissed or rejected, it's important to let the person know that you care about them and are there to support them. If they're minor, it's important to connect them with a medical and mental health care provider for evaluation. Effective treatments involve a combination of psychotherapy, nutrition counseling, and medical care. The main treatment is psychotherapy, specifically cognitive behavioral therapy. Mental health providers can help patients identify and reframe negative thoughts about body image and work towards developing a healthier relationship with food. In adults, antidepressant medication can be effective as part of the treatment for bulimia. Partnering with a medical provider and dietitian can help address some of the potential medical consequences of bulimia and establish healthy eating and exercise habits. For most people, treatment will take place in the clinic setting, though a small number will benefit from higher levels of care, like day programs, and rarely inpatient hospitalization. For the friends and family of those struggling with an eating disorder, seeing the eating disorder as something separate from their loved one is key in the recovery process. I find it helpful to imagine a Venn diagram where we have the eating disorder and the patient. When the eating disorder is strong, these two circles can really overlap, but over time we work to split them apart, and it starts with viewing the eating disorder as its own thing. Most patients will have bulimia for at least 12 months, and more than half will recover. The longer someone has an eating disorder, the lower the chance of recovery. Over time, about 1/3 will have a recurrence of their eating disorder. Help is available for those who need it. Talking to your primary care provider can be a great place to start. As someone who struggle with bulimia may also have other mental health diagnoses, it's important to seek help immediately if there's ever any concern for safety, like thoughts of hopelessness or suicide. I've taken care of many patients who have struggled with disordered eating who were able to recover and develop a healthy relationship with food and their bodies. Alice, whose story we shared earlier, was one of those fortunate ones. She was reluctant to talk to her parents at first, but eventually was able to open up to them about her eating disorder. She worked with a therapist, a dietitian, and her doctor for 2 years, and continues to see a therapist now that she's in college. Acknowledging the eating disorder thoughts can feel overwhelming and is an important first step towards getting help and beginning the recovery process. To get help or additional resources, please check in with your primary care provider.

Is Mental Health important​ in the workplace?  Tom explores all things related to workplace mental health, including mental health in school workplaces,  in this insightful video. Tom helps employers figure out mental health at work. He reviews workplaces, trains managers and writes plans. 
Since 2012 he has interviewed more than 130 people, surveyed thousands and worked across the UK with corporations, civil service, charities, the public sector, schools and small business. Tom has worked with national mental health charities Mind and Time to Change and consults widely across the UK. He lives in Norfolk and is mildly obsessed with cricket and camping.

He runs Bamboo Mental Health, an organisation dedicated to improving how employers support their people on mental health. This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx

Do you see yourself as overly sensitive? Do have intense emotional reactions that seem extreme and disproportionate to the event that triggered it? In Dialectical Behaviour Therapy (DBT) we often use the analogy of a burn or wound to help us understand how past trauma can increase sensitivity years later. When a wound is psychological the people around us often have no idea that they have touched on old wounds. So they can feel confused, fearful or angry when they witness the intense emotional reaction that appears to come out of nowhere.

If we have no idea how to heal those old wounds, it is understandable that we get to work hiding them or trying to numb the pain that they can trigger. And there are plenty of things that do just that. But none of them come without a cost. The price we pay is often in our relationships, mental and physical health, and ability to be at peace when all is still and silent.

description:
"Why is it that some people are more vulnerable to life's slings and arrows and others more resilient?" In this eye-opening talk, Richard Davidson discusses how mindfulness can improve well-being and outlines strategies to boost four components of a healthy mind: awareness, connection, insight, and purpose. 

Richard Davidson is researching how mindfulness changes the emotional life of our brains and what we know about people's brains of individuals showing more resilience than others. Davidson is Wiliam James and Vilas professor of psychology and psychiatry at the University of Wisconsin-Madison as well as founder and director of the Center for Healthy Minds. His research is focused on the neural bases of emotion and emotional style and methods to promote human flourishing, including meditation and related contemplative practices. #Neuroscience #Wellbeing #MentalHealth Richard Davidson is Research Professor of Psychology and Psychiatry and Founder & Director of the Center for Healthy Minds, University of Wisconsin-Madison.Davidson’s research is focused on the neural bases of emotion and emotional style and methods to promote human flourishing including meditation and related contemplative practices. Davidson has been recognized for his research through various awards, such as a National Institute of Mental Health Research Scientist Award and an  Established Investigator Award from the National Alliance for Research in Schizophrenia and Affective Disorders (NARSAD). Davidson received his Ph.D. from Harvard University in Psychology and has been teaching psychology and psychiatry at the University of Wisconsin-Madison since 1984. title: What medications should I continue or stop taking before a colonoscopy?
description:
Learn more about colonoscopy at http://www.YouAndColonoscopy.com  
In this video, Dr. Gelrud and Dr. Echavarria explain which medications should be continued, which ones should be adjusted in dosage, and which ones should be stopped before your colonoscopy. Be sure to tell your doctor well ahead of your colonoscopy about any regularly prescribed medications you are taking and any health conditions or allergies, as this information needs to be shared when you are booking your procedure. It is very important that you talk about this early and not the day before or the day of your procedure. Some medications may need to be adjusted prior to your colonoscopy, such as insulin, heart medications, or blood thinners. For your individual case, you should ask your doctor if you should continue with, adjust, or stop these medications.

title: What can I eat or drink before colonoscopy?
description:
Learn more about colonoscopy at http://www.YouAndColonoscopy.com
Colonoscopy bowel prep is a two-step process that involves dietary restrictions and taking a bowel prep medication. In this video, Dr. Echavarria and Dr. Gelrud discuss the dietary restrictions that are required before a colonoscopy. Three days before your colonoscopy, you will need to begin a low residue diet of foods that are very low in fiber and easy to digest (e.g., white bread, rice and pasta, plain crackers, canned fruit, lean meats without skin, and eggs). Do not eat seeds, green vegetables such as broccoli, cauliflower, kale, cabbage, and do not have dairy, or certain juices like prune juice. One day before ‒ and the day of ‒ your colonoscopy you will need to limit your diet to clear liquids only (e.g. clear broth, black tea or coffee, clear, light-colored juices, clear soft-drinks, clear sports drinks, plain gelatin without fruit, pulp-free juice bars, and water). Do not drink alcohol, liquids you can’t see through, dairy products, or red or purple liquids (these colors may be confused for blood during the colonoscopy). On the day of your colonoscopy, do not drink anything two hours before your procedure.

transcript_text: Getting ready for a colonoscopy can feel like a lot to manage and one of the biggest questions people have is about their medications. It is completely normal to wonder how your daily prescriptions might affect the process. For a safe and successful colonoscopy, you should always discuss all your current medications with your doctor well before your procedure. While your doctor will provide personalized instructions, critical medications that often requiring specific adjustments include blood thinners, also known as anti-coagulants or antiplatlets, and any medications for diabetes, such as insulin or oral agents. The primary reason certain medications need adjustment is to ensure your safety and the effectiveness of the colonoscopy. Blood thinners increase your risk of bleeding during the procedure if polyp are removed. So these often need to be paused or adjusted. Diabetes medications must be managed carefully to prevent dangerously low blood sugar levels while you are fasting and undergoing bowel preparation. Your health care team will provide a clear plan for medications like warpherin, aspirin, clitigil, or any insulin doses. It is also important to mention any iron supplements you take as these can leave a dark residue in your colon, making it harder for the doctor to see clearly during the examination. Additionally, certain vitamins, herbal remedies, and over-the-counter pain relievers like ibuprofen can sometimes have blood thinning effects. So, include them in your discussion. Never stop taking any medication without first getting specific guidance from your prescribing doctor or the gastroenterenterologist performing your colonoscopy. The crucial step is to create a complete and accurate list of everything you take, including prescriptions, over-the-counter medicines, supplements, and even vitamins. Share this list with your doctor during your pre-procedure consultation, allowing them ample time to develop a customized plan. This plan might involve temporarily stopping certain medications, adjusting dosages, or coordinating with other specialists like your cardiologist or endocrinologist. By proactively communicating with your health care team about your medication regimen, you are taking a vital step towards ensuring a smooth, safe, and effective colonoscopy. This careful planning helps ensure that your doctor has the best possible view, allowing for a thorough examination and peace of mind for you.

Keep taking all heart and blood pressure medications. Do not stop those medications. You can continue taking your aspirin. There is no need to stop that medication. And if you need to take any pain or anti-inflammatory medications, you can take those as well. If you're diabetic, speak to your healthcare provider about your diabetes medication. This is very important conversation that needs to be had. Up until this point, you've been able to eat a normal diet. But now, two days before your procedure, I want you to start on what's called a low residue diet. Foods that are low residue break down very easily and do not leave a lot of stool behind in the colon. Examples would be things like chicken, fish, rice, eggs, mashed potatoes. Things I want you to stay away from are things like fruit, and vegetables. They have a lot of fiber in them, and they're very slow to break down. description:
For many people, one of the most uncomfortable parts of a colonoscopy is the preparation for the procedure.

description:
Hello, my name is Deanna and I am an anesthesia provider here at The Everett Clinic. I'm here to provide you with a brief overview of the sedation that you may receive for your colonoscopy and/or endoscopy. This video is meant as an introduction. You'll have an opportunity to speak in person with your gastroenterologist and sedation nurse immediately before your procedure to ask questions or discuss concerns that you may have. Most people undergoing colonoscopy and/or endoscopy will receive sedation through their IV. Many people do not remember having their procedure because of the sedation given. 

Some people don't even remember talking with their gastroenterologist but rest assured your doctor will give you written instruction and the results of your exam so that you have that information available once your sedation wears off. If you wish to be more awake or more asleep for your procedure then please let your nurse and physician know so they can adjust the amount of sedation to better match your wishes. Common drugs used are Propofol, Midazolam and occasionally Fentanyl. If you have allergies or concerns about what medicine will be used then please tell your nurse and physician when they meet you prior to your procedure. For most people, the sedation wears off quickly and you'll feel mostly back to normal within an hour or two. While you may feel normal, we instruct people to refrain from driving or making critical decisions for the remainder of the day. following your sedation as some people may still feel slightly impaired without realizing it.

I'm Dr. Matt Deppe, I'm a general surgeon
with Mayo Clinic Health System and one of the areas that are of particular interest
and passion is in colorectal cancer prevention. I think there are few things
that patients don't know about colonoscopy and about colon cancer
screening, that might alleviate a bit of concern or help them make better
decisions about choosing to do a colonoscopy or choosing the screening
technique that's right for them. I think one of the things patients don't realize
is how far the equipment has come technologically, in our system we use
the 190 series Olympus equipment, which is the newest on the market and has a
lot of features that help us keep patients more comfortable as we do the
examination. Our typical patient, who should be
screened for colon cancer, is any patient over age 50. There are patients, however,
who have a family history of colon cancer, in which, depending upon when
they're their relative had colon cancer, we'll recommend it at an earlier age, but
of course any patient who has symptoms, blood within their stool, as an example,
are patients who we more urgently push to consider colonoscopy  for safety
reasons. Colonoscopy begins with a patient taking
a preparation which is medication that's taken by mouth, to clear out the colon,
clearly the least pleasant portion of the procedure. Most patients come in and
they think that there's more discomfort ahead, and certainly sometimes
exams can be more difficult than we anticipate, but usually they're not. Usually patients are are surprised to find they have no discomfort, and my favorite phrase, you're done already? Which I really enjoy and I think all of our
endoscopists do. So we have several options for
anesthesia. Our most common choice is what's called conscious sedation that
involves, for most practitioners, a medication called Versed and also a pain
medication called Fentanyl and they're both designed to be effective very
quickly and very reliably effective and very short duration, in that they wear
off very quickly and we can predict how long they'll be within that patient
system. That being said, about 10% of our patients will choose to have no
medication for their colostomy and of course if we think that that's not a
great idea, we will advise them otherwise, but for most patients who choose that
they have a pleasant experience and are comfortable throughout the examination
and are able to essentially leave immediately after the examinations
finished. We also have a third option which is anesthesia provided by our
anesthesia practitioners and that means a deeper form of anesthesia there are
some benefits to it and some negatives to it as well and and some patients will
choose that option because of previous experience
with Colonoscopy or other anesthetic experiences. I think another thing
patients don't realize is that recovery is very quick. Perhaps years ago, it was
several hours of trying to pass gas trying to feel less bloated waiting for
medication to wear off. Now we use carbon dioxide, in order to
see within the colon. What that means is that it absorbs in just a matter of
minutes. So patients, even a half-hour after the examination, no longer feel
bloated and feel normal. So our patients are staying much less,
for a much shorter duration, in our recovery area after the procedure and
are able to go home feeling normal. The common concerns that we have
from patients are will I have more discomfort than I anticipate? Will it
be difficult for me to get through the examination? Will I be bloated
for hours after the examination, as an example, and I think the thing that
patients find most comforting, is not only the experience of their friends and
family, who undergo the examination, now, and temporarily, but as we start the
examination some patients may choose to be awake to see what it feels like to
start with and often those of the patients who are flabbergasted when
we've completed the examination and the first thing they do is tell their
friends. I think the important thing when it
comes to colorectal cancer prevention is do something. Colonoscopy is, for many
people, the best test in the best option and as the end evaluation, the end tool,
that we have to evaluate the positive result results from some of our other
screening examinations but the key is do something this is a condition that in
many cases is preventable. Why not?

transcript_text: Hi, my name is Sarah Boostrom. I'm a colorectal surgeon with Baylor Scott & White, and today we are going to dispel some myths regarding colonoscopy and explain why the jitters are far worse than the procedure. The most common fear regarding colonoscopy is the bowel preparation, the cleaning out for the procedure. This is required in order to allow your proceduralist to see the lining of the colon in order to see all polyps. Polyps can be removed if seen, and the better bowel preparation allows the proceduralist to see the smallest of polyps. Another misconception is needing to take a lot of time off of work. In fact, the only day required to take off is the day of the procedure. The entire time spent at the outpatient facility is approximately 1.5 hours. Following that, patients are allowed to leave the facility with a family member or friend. They are allowed to eat and return to normal activities, including work, the following day. Another misconception regarding colonoscopy screening as well as diagnostic is expense. Most insurance carriers will cover a screening colonoscopy at 100%. The final fear regarding colonoscopy is embarrassment. In fact, there should be no embarrassment with this procedure. It is a very common procedure performed daily. The patient is covered the entire time. Finally, the benefits of colonoscopy outweigh the risks. Not only can a screening colonoscopy be diagnostic, but it can also be therapeutic and preventive. By removing polyps, colon cancers cannot grow. This allows for patients to prevent developing a cancer of the colon or the rectum, which is the second leading cause of cancer death. If you would like to learn if you are at risk of colorectal cancer, please contact your local provider.

title: What happens when bowel prep fails before a colonoscopy? #nurse #nhs #colonoscopy #preparation

A channel that discusses clear, simple guidance on gut health and endoscopy care through the lens of a Nurse. 

https://linktr.ee/alajembachdera
transcript_text: So you drank all the bowel prep until your bowel wasn't clean enough and the colonoscopy did not go ahead. What happens next? When your bowel isn't clean properly, the doctors won't be able to see clearly and that could mean missed polyp or missed cancers which is very risky both for you and for the clinician. So when you have got a poor bow preparation, it doesn't call for you to be stressed rather you should understand that it is common occurrences in in endoscopy. So what happens next? The first step is that you would get an urgent date to have the colonoscopy done again, especially if your colonoscopy was referred via the fasttrack pathway. Secondly is that your your nurses or doctors would consider giving you a stronger laxative and changing the protocol for you and this could mean um initiating what we call a split dose. This means that you take the first dose of your laxative the day before the procedure and the second dose on the day of your actual procedure. It also means that you have to go on a longer and stricter diet plan. So you have to go for example 7 days of um low residue diets and drinking lots of fluid. Something also that could be considered by your um healthcare provider is that they could give you an extended bowel preparation. This is where you take some stool softeners especially if you have got constipation a history of constipation um 7 days before you take your actual laxatives. So all of these options are still available and on the table for you to have your bowel cleaned properly. I know it's stressful. It is something we contend every day in clinic. But try as much as possible to comply to the instructions so as for you to have a successful investigation. And one more thing is that if after all of this your bowel keeps failing and the doctors could consider an alternative investigation.

transcript_text: Imagine having a powerful tool to protect your health, a way to catch potential issues early before they become bigger problems. When it comes to something as important as colon health, proactive steps can make all the difference, offering both peace of mind and potentially life-saving benefits. The good news is yes, Medicare does indeed cover routine colon cancer screenings. This includes a variety of tests designed to detect colon cancer early, even before symptoms appear. This coverage reflects Medicare's commitment to preventive care. Recognizing that early detection significantly improves treatment outcomes and can save lives, Medicare's coverage for these screenings is rooted in a clear understanding of the benefits of early detection. For most people, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and other health organizations recommend starting regular colon cancer screenings at age 45. The goal is to find precancerous polyp and remove them before they can turn into cancer or to discover cancer at an early highly treatable stage. This proactive approach by Medicare helps ensure beneficiaries have access to these vital preventative services aligning with current medical guidelines that emphasize regular checkups for long-term health. To take advantage of this coverage, you should talk to your doctor about your personal risk factors and which screening test is right for you. Medicare covers several types of screenings, including colonoscopies, stool-based tests like the fecal occult blood test or fecal imuninochemical test, and sometimes virtual colonoscopies, also known as CT colonography. For a colonoscopy, Medicare covers the procedure at no cost to you if you are aged 45 or older. If a polip is found and removed during your screening colonoscopy, it is still considered a screening procedure and typically there is no out-ofpocket cost for the procedure itself. It is important to remember that Medicare PartB covers these preventative services. An interesting detail to note is that if a screening colonoscopy turns into a diagnostic one because of findings like polyp, the cost structure typically does not change for the procedure. itself, reflecting Medicare's strong support for preventative care. For other screening tests, like the stool-based options, they are also covered periodically, offering flexible choices depending on your health needs and your doctor's recommendations. Understanding these details can help you plan your health care effectively. Ultimately, Medicare's comprehensive coverage for routine colon cancer screenings empowers you to be proactive about your health. By covering these essential tests, Medicare helps remove financial barriers, making it easier for you to access screenings that can detect cancer early or prevent it altogether. title: Does Medicare Pay For A Colonoscopy?

Colorectal cancer is the third leading cause of cancer-related deaths in the United States.

Colonoscopies are important screenings that help in the early detection and prevention of colorectal cancer, especially as we get older.
