title: Colorectal cancer screening
description: Learn about the 2 types of screening tests for colorectal cancer – Fecal Immunochemical Test (FIT) and colonoscopy. You may be referred for a colonoscopy if you have an abnormal FIT result.
channel_description:
MyHealth.Alberta.ca is a Government of Alberta initiative in partnership with Alberta Health Services. Videos on the MyHealth.Alberta.ca channel were developed in consultation with Alberta health professionals.  

The MyHealth.Alberta.ca website provides a single source of trusted health information for Albertans.
transcript_text:
Colorectal cancer is one of the most 
common causes of cancer deaths in Alberta. Most cases are in people over 50 years 
old, with no family history of the disease. Colorectal cancer is cancer of the colon, 
the large intestine, or the rectum. If you’re 50 to 74, it’s important 
to get screened regularly. Screening looks for early signs of cancer in 
people who feel well and have no symptoms. Screening is the best way to find colorectal 
cancer early when treatment is most effective. Most colorectal cancers begin as growths called 
“polyps” on the inner wall of the colon or rectum. Not all polyps turn into cancer, 
but some types can with time. Early-stage colorectal cancer and polyps 
can exist for years, without symptoms. With regular screening, colorectal 
cancer can be found early, and many   types of polyps can be removed 
before they turn into cancer. The 2 main screening tests 
for colorectal cancer are   Fecal Immunochemical Test or FIT and colonoscopy. You and your healthcare provider can 
discuss which test is right for you. FIT is the recommended screening test for people 
at average risk of getting colorectal cancer. Most people are at average risk. This includes those with no symptoms and no 
personal or family history of colorectal cancer. Start screening with FIT at age 50. FIT is an easy, at-home test that 
checks for hidden blood in your stool. You collect a small stool 
sample and it’s sent to the lab. If your FIT result is normal, it means that 
no blood was found in your stool sample. You should continue to screen with FIT regularly. If your FIT result is abnormal, it means 
that blood was found in your stool sample. This can happen for different reasons. While most people with an abnormal result do 
not have cancer, your doctor or healthcare   provider may recommend a colonoscopy 
to find the cause of the bleeding. Looking at the numbers, if 100 people 
get a colonoscopy after an abnormal FIT,   about 2 to 3 will be diagnosed 
with colorectal cancer. When colorectal cancer is found early, 
90% of cases can be treated successfully. This is why screening is so important. Colonoscopy is the recommended test for people at 
an increased risk of getting colorectal cancer. You may be at increased risk if you or 
someone in your family such as a parent,   sibling, or child had colorectal 
cancer or polyps in the past. A colonoscopy lets the doctor 
see the inside of your colon. This test is done using a colonoscope,   which is a long, thin, flexible tube 
with a light and camera on the end. Remember, never ignore new symptoms 
including blood in your stool,   a change in your bowel habits, pain in 
your belly, or unexplained weight loss. See your doctor or healthcare provider if   you develop these or any other 
symptoms you’re worried about. For more information visit ahs.ca/colonoscopy.​​

title: Screening for Colorectal Cancer
description:
MEDICAL ANIMATION TRANSCRIPT:  Screening for colorectal cancer means looking for signs of cancer in your large intestine before you have symptoms. Screening can help find cancer at an early stage. This can make treating it easier because the cancer might not have spread. Screening for colorectal cancer is recommended for everyone, beginning at age 45. You may need screening earlier and more often if you or your family has a history of colorectal cancer or diseases that inflame your bowel. Some tests screen for colorectal cancer by looking inside your large intestine. These tests include sigmoidoscopy, colonoscopy, and colonography. A sigmoidoscopy views the lower third of your large intestine using a camera on the end of a flexible tube. The tube is inserted through your anus into your large intestine to look for polyps and other signs of cancer. A colonoscopy also views your large intestine using a similar camera, but it looks along the entire length of your large intestine for polyps or other signs of cancer. A colonography, also known as virtual colonoscopy, uses CT scans of your large intestine. A computer uses the scans to make a three-dimensional view inside your large intestine to look for signs of cancer. Other tests screen for colorectal cancer by looking at your stools or feces. Fecal blood tests look for traces of blood in stool samples. These tests are often done in combination with the sigmoidoscopy. Blood in your stool may be a sign of polyps in your colon or cancer. However, stool blood may have other causes that aren't cancer. Talk to your healthcare provider about what your test results mean. In a stool DNA test, a stool sample is checked for abnormal DNA from polyps or cancer. If you have questions about these tests or your test results, talk to your doctor.

Their goal was to go from a screening uptake of 59% nationally to 80% nationally from the year 2014 to the year 2018. What they noticed in reviewing the data, the national data on screening rates, was that screening rates had plateaued in the United States at in around 2013. Around 2013 is also when we had increased access to health insurance and also more awareness about preventive medicine. So, the National Colorectal Cancer Roundtable partnered with the American Cancer Society, the CDC, other organizations, and started this campaign in March of 2014. Since that time, the campaign has been endorsed by over 1,500 organizations and institutions. They have They have initiated targeted efforts and funding to improve screening, specifically focusing on populations in which there was low participation in screening. And as part Their efforts were recognized and included in the Cancer Moonshot 2020. I want to share with you what some of the key components of this campaign are. So, the first thing that they dedicated themselves to doing was to make the campaign go viral. And I'll share with you some examples of how they did that. They had a state-by-state approach. So, they had representatives in every state and actually every US territory from the National Colorectal Cancer Roundtable to promote awareness about colorectal cancer and to work towards this goal of 80%. They engaged health care plans, hospitals. They also engaged cancer centers around the country. They had strong leadership um involvement. And that's from organizations to hospitals and also um places or companies or organizations like the American Cancer Society. They worked in certain settings to help reduce the financial barriers to screening, in some settings doing things like reducing the cost of a FIT kit or making free colonoscopy available. They also, in all of their efforts, and this is very important, have emphasized both colonoscopy and stool testing. So, they did not go around preaching that everybody needed a colonoscopy. They went around preaching specifically that the best test is the test that gets done. And saying that we want everyone to be screened, and we think that stool testing is an appropriate way to get to our 80%. They used tailored messaging to reach the unscreened, and they also emphasize evidence-based interventions that appear in the literature. So, this is their pledge. They wrote a pledge, and it's a one-page document that includes their commitment, and they ask organizations and institutions to sign this pledge that says that their organization will do everything they can to reach 80% screened by the year 2018. And this was widely circu- circulated across the country. All of these organizations took the pledge. As I mentioned, 1,500 organizations. And you'll see included in this list are um major medical associations, including our GI organizations, the ACG, the AGA, and the ASGE. The pledge was also taken in all US territories, so all 50 states, DC, Guam, and Puerto Rico. In addition, they uh took advantage of some celebrity appeal. So, Katie Couric was one of their main spokespeople, and they had national televised events, workshops, roundtables to spread awareness about colon cancer. They had events in certain parts of the country where they had mayors sign formal proclamations of the 80 by 8 by 2018 campaign, again to increase awareness and the profile of the campaign. And they had special events. One of them was called Light Up Chicago, where they had buildings literally display the hashtag 80 by 2018. And there was a day where even Niagara Falls turned blue in support of colorectal cancer screening. Where are we now in this campaign? Is what we'll talk about next. This includes Medicare Advantage plans, community health centers, commercial health plans, and medical practices and health systems. Uh the Veterans Affairs, for example, is one of the organizations that actually reached 80% um well before the goal of 2018. And that's something that we're actually very proud of in the VA. What the American Cancer Society and National Colorectal Cance- Cancer Roundtable predicted was that if we are able to keep the ski- screening prevalence at the 2015 rates rather than the 2013 rates, we will s- have an additional um rescue of lives. So, for example, about 39,000 people or cases of colorectal cancer will be prevented, and almost about 39 or 37,000 cases of death from colon cancer will be averted. So, again, huge impact from just additional screening. Another population that they were particular interested in was the federally qualified health center population. So, federally qualified health centers in the United States take care of the 26 million under- insured and under-served individuals. And the screening rates in this population were the lowest. In some of the FQHCs at the beginning of this effort, the screening rate was 14%. And what they were able to show through data, we actually call it the Uniform Data Systems, was that there was a 5% increase overall um in screening rates since the start of the campaign. And as you can see, from the time that the campaign started in 2014 to 2016 in this infographic, there was a rise in the screening rate, which we again attribute to some of this effort. So, we're not quite there yet. Uh we actually won't know what the screening rate in 2018 is until 2020, because that's how data work. Uh and I think with further analysis of data from the CDC uh and from um NHANES and NHIS and BRFSS, we'll be able to tell where we are um hopefully by December 31st, 2018, which is the deadline. And these three factors all together contribute to whether to uptake of colorectal cancer screening, meaning whether a person does or does not get screened. So, for example, some of the patient factors include uh health beliefs, uh uh whether or not a patient has insurance, there's fear of a colorectal cancer diagnosis, which we call cancer fatalism, which is actually this concept that patients may be fearful of just being diagnosed of a cancer, and because of that, they won't participate in screening. In addition to these patient factor, provider factors include knowledge of screening guidelines, and whether a provider, particularly primary care providers, recommend screening. System-level factors um are broader, right? Cuz they're across the health care system. And they include uh access to primary care, access to gastroenterologists and and colonoscopy, systems that use reminder systems for colonoscopy screening are more likely to have their patients undergo screening than systems that don't. All of these factors work together in in helping promote or discourage screening among our patients. One that I'd like to highlight is a provider recommendation for screening. Specifically, this is a survey that's administered to Californians via telephone. Looking at this survey, we actually queried the survey for people who were non-adherent to colorectal cancer screening. This is one of many studies that highlights the importance of provider recommendation for screening. And that is at the MD level, that's at the NP level, that's whoever these patients consider is their primary care provider is essential in providing this information about screening and encouraging patients that they go participate in screening. When we talk specifically about screening colonoscopy, we know that that there are specific barriers and challenges. So, we've probably all heard many of our patients say that they're fearful of the discomfort from a colonoscopy. Um maybe they're not able to take time off of work or bring an escort with them to the procedure. Um in some cases, especially if there's a positive FIT that precedes the colonoscopy, there's an out-of-pocket cost that patients are wary of. Another reason why I think it's important to highlight to patients that there are other mechan- mechanisms other than colonoscopy. Colonoscopy might not be feasible for So, my last section here, I want to talk a little bit about some of the strategies that I think will become important as we try to completely close this screening gap. In other words, bring us up to a screening rate of 80% nationally. We will achieve this goal only by working together. And by working together, I mean everything from the academic setting to the community, from the health systems and hospitals to the organizations that help promote help us promote awareness. So, in getting to 80%, one of the things that will become essential is improving access to screening tests. So, in academic settings, often patients have access to colonoscopy. If not colonoscopy, home-based stool tests. In community settings, a community health centers or federally qualified health centers, there are actually some settings in which access to even stool-based testing is difficult, or settings where the systems or the centers are using outdated methods, so using very old FOBT kits that probably are not the best method for screening. So, that's one thing that we need to work on. We need to work on messaging to specific populations. So, I opened by telling you a little bit about some of the disparities we see in screening, and I highlighted that for Hispanic or Latino Americans, the screening rates are the lowest. So, organizations like the American Cancer Society have made tailored messaging in pamphlets and in video form that's available in Spanish and in English to Hispanic patients to talk about the importance of screening. And we use a lot of these, especially in the work that we do in the community, to educate about screening. We need to work on improving operational efficiencies about around screening. And a lot of the work at UCLA actually right now is about coordination of care in these efforts. So, for example, automatization of screening orders. So, maybe in some systems having it so that as soon as the patient turns 50, they're automatically sent a FIT kit or automatically sent a letter inviting them to schedule a colonoscopy. Uh we've also seen um the use of this program called the flu FIT program. I don't know if any of you are well aware of it. It was actually um Michael Potter Potter, who's a family medicine physician at UCSF, came up with the concept of combining getting your flu shot with being handed a FIT kit. And this is what they do in his health system. When you come for a flu shot, you walk out with a FIT kit. And they've actually been able to increase their screening rates at UCSF significantly just by coupling those two annual um requests. I think it's also going to be important um to get to 80% that we improve coordination of care. So, there are a lot of examples of use of patient navigators to help patients not only with participating in screening, but getting the colon prep right for the colonoscopy or following up with the colonoscopy after the FIT is positive. And also staff coordination. So, in the VA in particular, we do not we do not focus just on the primary care doctors to get the screening done. In most cases in the VA, it's a it's a nurse practitioner who's doing the education about screening and handing the patients a FIT kit. Lastly, I want to highlight again that I think it's going to be very important for us to encourage various screening options. So, rather than talking only about colonoscopy, teaching patients that there are other options for them to get screened. So, we say FIT and colonoscopy or we say consider some of the other screening options. As I mentioned earlier, Cologuard, which is the FIT DNA test, C2 colonography, or Septin9, which is the serum screening test. Now, I want to be clear that right now the Septin9 is not approved for primary screening. Um right now it's FDA-approved to be used for screening in cases where other modalities of screening cannot be achieved. But, I do think we're moving closer to um blood testing for several types of cancer. Every system that we know of now that has reached 80% is relying on stool-based testing in addition to colonoscopy. And this is an important point. We for a long time have preached colonoscopy, and I think we need to recognize to get to that 80% is a high number. And to get 80% of your population screened, it's not very likely that everyone is going to be interested in a colonoscopy. So, we need to broaden the way we think, and we need to understand that there are other ways to get there. And also recognize using real-life data that often we're going to have to use other mechanisms for screening other than colonoscopy. Lastly, I just want everyone to know that there are several um ways that you can get further patient education and outreach about colorectal cancer screening. So, these are some of the references or resources that I like. The American Cancer Society has videos, pamphlets, brochures. They have um all kinds of information that you can have available in your office that you can send to patients. It's tailored, so they have general information, they have information that's tailored to specific racial or ethnic groups, different languages, and it's all available for free on their website. So, I like to remind people that that's there. You don't need to recreate the wheel, and um you don't need to explain everything to everyone in every appointment. You can definitely have these materials available for your patients as they come see you in your office. In summary, I just want to highlight that colorectal cancer continues to be a high-burden disease here in the United States. This 80% by 2018 campaign has really helped propel us towards this national goal of screening 80% of our population. I'm not quite sure we'll get there. We won't know again until probably 2020 what our 2018 rates are, but I do know it's helped. And I know that the gains that we've seen in the last 5 years or so are probably attributed to this effort. Even beyond 2018, we're still going to have a lot of work to do. Every year, there's hundreds of thousands of people that turn 50. So, there's a brand new population to educate. And lastly, I'd like to make the point that we must continue to target patient, provider, and system-level barriers like the ones we've we've spoken about today to colorectal cancer screening if we want to get to that goal. Thank you very much.

Now, the combined mechanism of FIT plus flexical sigmoidoscopy recommends that the flex sig occurs every 10 years and the FIT occurs every year. With the introduction of screening in the United States, we've seen a significant reduction of mortality from colorectal cancer. As you can see here, there's been a percent decline per decade in mortality since 1970s. And that percent decline has increased with each decade. So, the most recent decade, which is 2000 to 2010, we've seen a 25% reduction in mortality from colorectal cancer. We think that this mortality improvement is in large part due to increased uptake of colorectal cancer screening. Our screening rate in this country, according to Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System data, was about 37% in the year 2000 and increased to about 65% in the year 2012. Despite the improvement in screening rates over time, screening rates for colorectal cancer remain suboptimal. When compared to other malignancies that we screen for, including prostate cancer, breast cancer, and cervical cancer, screening rates for colon cancer, which are marked by the black arrow in this slide, are much lower. So again, much much room for improvement, especially when compared to other malignancies. In addition, there are significant disparities or differences by patient characteristics in screening uptake. So, this looks at racial and ethnic disparities here in this slide. And what you can see is the screening rates for colorectal cancer in the United States are lowest for Hispanics or Latino Americans compared to other ethnic groups. We think that this screening disparity in part explains some of the disparities in colorectal cancer outcomes that we see. So, for example, African Americans have the highest mortality rate from colorectal cancer in the United States and they have lower screening rates than white Americans. Hispanic Americans have the lowest rates of colorectal cancer in the United States, but they have higher mortality from colorectal cancer than white Americans. And we think that that difference is in part explained by the low screening uptake among Latinos. So, this brings us to why the National Colorectal Roundtable engaged in the 80% by 2018 campaign, which we'll talk about next. This campaign was started by the National Colorectal Cancer Roundtable in March of 2014. Their goal was to reduce the burden of colorectal cancer by increasing screening uptake. Their goal was to go from a screening uptake of 59% nationally to 80% nationally from the year 2014 to the year 2018. What they noticed in reviewing the data, the national data on screening rates, was that screening rates had plateaued in the United States at in around 2013. Around 2013 is also when we had increased access to health insurance and also more awareness about preventive medicine. So, the National Colorectal Cancer Roundtable partnered with the American Cancer Society, the CDC, other organizations, and started this campaign in March of 2014. Since that time, the campaign has been endorsed by over 1,500 organizations and institutions. They have They have initiated targeted efforts and funding to improve screening, specifically focusing on populations in which there was low participation in screening. And as part Their efforts were recognized and included in the Cancer Moonshot 2020. I want to share with you what some of the key components of this campaign are. So, the first thing that they dedicated themselves to doing was to make the campaign go viral. And I'll share with you some examples of how they did that. They had a state-by-state approach. So, they had representatives in every state and actually every US territory from the National Colorectal Cancer Roundtable to promote awareness about colorectal cancer and to work towards this goal of 80%. They engaged health care plans, hospitals. They also engaged cancer centers around the country. They had strong leadership um involvement. And that's from organizations to hospitals and also um places or companies or organizations like the American Cancer Society. They worked in certain settings to help reduce the financial barriers to screening, in some settings doing things like reducing the cost of a FIT kit or making free colonoscopy available. They also, in all of their efforts, and this is very important, have emphasized both colonoscopy and stool testing. So, they did not go around preaching that everybody needed a colonoscopy. They went around preaching specifically that the best test is the test that gets done. And saying that we want everyone to be screened, and we think that stool testing is an appropriate way to get to our 80%. They used tailored messaging to reach the unscreened, and they also emphasize evidence-based interventions that appear in the literature. So, this is their pledge. They wrote a pledge, and it's a one-page document that includes their commitment, and they ask organizations and institutions to sign this pledge that says that their organization will do everything they can to reach 80% screened by the year 2018. And this was widely circu- circulated across the country. All of these organizations took the pledge. As I mentioned, 1,500 organizations. And you'll see included in this list are um major medical associations, including our GI organizations, the ACG, the AGA, and the ASGE. The pledge was also taken in all US territories, so all 50 states, DC, Guam, and Puerto Rico. In addition, they uh took advantage of some celebrity appeal. So, Katie Couric was one of their main spokespeople, and they had national televised events, workshops, roundtables to spread awareness about colon cancer. They had events in certain parts of the country where they had mayors sign formal proclamations of the 80 by 8 by 2018 campaign, again to increase awareness and the profile of the campaign. And they had special events. One of them was called Light Up Chicago, where they had buildings literally display the hashtag 80 by 2018. And there was a day where even Niagara Falls turned blue in support of colorectal cancer screening. Where are we now in this campaign? Is what we'll talk about next. Since the launch of the campaign in 2014, several organizations that I mentioned have taken the pledge. And among those organizations, several have reached already this goal of 80%. This includes Medicare Advantage plans, community health centers, commercial health plans, and medical practices and health systems. Uh the Veterans Affairs, for example, is one of the organizations that actually reached 80% um well before the goal of 2018. And that's something that we're actually very proud of in the VA. The gains in screening also include a 5% increase in screening rates nationally between 2013 and 2015, which is about 4 million additional adults screened. What the American Cancer Society and National Colorectal Cance- Cancer Roundtable predicted was that if we are able to keep the ski- screening prevalence at the 2015 rates rather than the 2013 rates, we will s- have an additional um rescue of lives. So, for example, about 39,000 people or cases of colorectal cancer will be prevented, and almost about 39 or 37,000 cases of death from colon cancer will be averted. So, again, huge impact from just additional screening. Another population that they were particular interested in was the federally qualified health center population. So, federally qualified health centers in the United States take care of the 26 million under- insured and under-served individuals. And the screening rates in this population were the lowest. In some of the FQHCs at the beginning of this effort, the screening rate was 14%. And what they were able to show through data, we actually call it the Uniform Data Systems, was that there was a 5% increase overall um in screening rates since the start of the campaign. And as you can see, from the time that the campaign started in 2014 to 2016 in this infographic, there was a rise in the screening rate, which we again attribute to some of this effort. So, we're not quite there yet. Uh we actually won't know what the screening rate in 2018 is until 2020, because that's how data work. But we think that we're moving in the right direction, and our estimate is that we're somewhere in the mid-70% nationally. Uh and I think with further analysis of data from the CDC uh and from um NHANES and NHIS and BRFSS, we'll be able to tell where we are um hopefully by December 31st, 2018, which is the deadline. Because we're not there, it's important for us to recognize that there continue to be significant barriers to screening. And I want to spend the next couple minutes talking about what we've learned about barriers to colorectal cancer screening. I like to think of barriers to screening as in three categories. And and part of this um method of categorization is is based off the Institute of Medicine and how they uh look at some health care problems and health care disparities. We know that there are patient-level factors. We know that there are also provider and system-level factors. And these three factors all together contribute to whether to uptake of colorectal cancer screening, meaning whether a person does or does not get screened. So, for example, some of the patient factors include uh health beliefs, uh uh whether or not a patient has insurance, there's fear of a colorectal cancer diagnosis, which we call cancer fatalism, which is actually this concept that patients may be fearful of just being diagnosed of a cancer, and because of that, they won't participate in screening. In addition to these patient factor, provider factors include knowledge of screening guidelines, and whether a provider, particularly primary care providers, recommend screening. System-level factors um are broader, right? Cuz they're across the health care system. And they include uh access to primary care, access to gastroenterologists and and colonoscopy, systems that use reminder systems for colonoscopy screening are more likely to have their patients undergo screening than systems that don't. All of these factors work together in in helping promote or discourage screening among our patients. One that I'd like to highlight is a provider recommendation for screening. So, this is a study that we did at UCLA a few years ago, and we looked at data from the California Health Interview Survey. Specifically, this is a survey that's administered to Californians via telephone. Looking at this survey, we actually queried the survey for people who were non-adherent to colorectal cancer screening. So, we took all the people who were unscreened, and we asked those people, "What is the one most important reason why you have not been screened for colorectal cancer?" What we found is overall in the survey, about 43% of people were unscreened. And in answering that question, 20% of people said that the number one reason why they have not been screened was because their provider, their doctor, never told them that they needed to be screened. This is one of many studies that highlights the importance of provider recommendation for screening. And that is at the MD level, that's at the NP level, that's whoever these patients consider is their primary care provider is essential in providing this information about screening and encouraging patients that they go participate in screening. When we talk specifically about screening colonoscopy, we know that that there are specific barriers and challenges. So, we've probably all heard many of our patients say that they're fearful of the discomfort from a colonoscopy. Um maybe they're not able to take time off of work or bring an escort with them to the procedure. Um in some cases, especially if there's a positive FIT that precedes the colonoscopy, there's an out-of-pocket cost that patients are wary of. These are challenges that are specific to screening, but even more specific to colonoscopy, and make it difficult for us to focus specifically on colonoscopy as the one method of screening. Another reason why I think it's important to highlight to patients that there are other mechan- mechanisms other than colonoscopy. Colonoscopy might not be feasible for So, my last section here, I want to talk a little bit about some of the strategies that I think will become important as we try to completely close this screening gap. In other words, bring us up to a screening rate of 80% nationally. We will achieve this goal only by working together. And by working together, I mean everything from the academic setting to the community, from the health systems and hospitals to the organizations that help promote help us promote awareness. So, in getting to 80%, one of the things that will become essential is improving access to screening tests. So, in academic settings, often patients have access to colonoscopy. If not colonoscopy, home-based stool tests. In community settings, a community health centers or federally qualified health centers, there are actually some settings in which access to even stool-based testing is difficult, or settings where the systems or the centers are using outdated methods, so using very old FOBT kits that probably are not the best method for screening. So, that's one thing that we need to work on. We need to work on messaging to specific populations. So, I opened by telling you a little bit about some of the disparities we see in screening, and I highlighted that for Hispanic or Latino Americans, the screening rates are the lowest. So, organizations like the American Cancer Society have made tailored messaging in pamphlets and in video form that's available in Spanish and in English to Hispanic patients to talk about the importance of screening. And we use a lot of these, especially in the work that we do in the community, to educate about screening. We need to work on improving operational efficiencies about around screening. And a lot of the work at UCLA actually right now is about coordination of care in these efforts. So, for example, automatization of screening orders. So, maybe in some systems having it so that as soon as the patient turns 50, they're automatically sent a FIT kit or automatically sent a letter inviting them to schedule a colonoscopy. Uh we've also seen um the use of this program called the flu FIT program. I don't know if any of you are well aware of it. It was actually um Michael Potter Potter, who's a family medicine physician at UCSF, came up with the concept of combining getting your flu shot with being handed a FIT kit. And this is what they do in his health system. When you come for a flu shot, you walk out with a FIT kit. And they've actually been able to increase their screening rates at UCSF significantly just by coupling those two annual um requests. I think it's also going to be important um to get to 80% that we improve coordination of care. So, there are a lot of examples of use of patient navigators to help patients not only with participating in screening, but getting the colon prep right for the colonoscopy or following up with the colonoscopy after the FIT is positive. And also staff coordination. So, in the VA in particular, we do not we do not focus just on the primary care doctors to get the screening done. In most cases in the VA, it's a it's a nurse practitioner who's doing the education about screening and handing the patients a FIT kit. Lastly, I want to highlight again that I think it's going to be very important for us to encourage various screening options. So, rather than talking only about colonoscopy, teaching patients that there are other options for them to get screened. So, we say FIT and colonoscopy or we say consider some of the other screening options. As I mentioned earlier, Cologuard, which is the FIT DNA test, C2 colonography, or Septin9, which is the serum screening test. Now, I want to be clear that right now the Septin9 is not approved for primary screening. Um right now it's FDA-approved to be used for screening in cases where other modalities of screening cannot be achieved. But, I do think we're moving closer to um blood testing for several types of cancer. Every system that we know of now that has reached 80% is relying on stool-based testing in addition to colonoscopy. And this is an important point. We for a long time have preached colonoscopy, and I think we need to recognize to get to that 80% is a high number. And to get 80% of your population screened, it's not very likely that everyone is going to be interested in a colonoscopy. So, we need to broaden the way we think, and we need to understand that there are other ways to get there. And also recognize using real-life data that often we're going to have to use other mechanisms for screening other than colonoscopy. Lastly, I just want everyone to know that there are several um ways that you can get further patient education and outreach about colorectal cancer screening. So, these are some of the references or resources that I like. The American Cancer Society has videos, pamphlets, brochures. They have um all kinds of information that you can have available in your office that you can send to patients. It's tailored, so they have general information, they have information that's tailored to specific racial or ethnic groups, different languages, and it's all available for free on their website. So, I like to remind people that that's there. You don't need to recreate the wheel, and um you don't need to explain everything to everyone in every appointment. You can definitely have these materials available for your patients as they come see you in your office. In summary, I just want to highlight that colorectal cancer continues to be a high-burden disease here in the United States. This 80% by 2018 campaign has really helped propel us towards this national goal of screening 80% of our population. I'm not quite sure we'll get there. We won't know again until probably 2020 what our 2018 rates are, but I do know it's helped. And I know that the gains that we've seen in the last 5 years or so are probably attributed to this effort. Even beyond 2018, we're still going to have a lot of work to do. Every year, there's hundreds of thousands of people that turn 50. So, there's a brand new population to educate. And lastly, I'd like to make the point that we must continue to target patient, provider, and system-level barriers like the ones we've we've spoken about today to colorectal cancer screening if we want to get to that goal. Thank you very much.

transcript_text: Preparing for a colonoscopy involves many steps from dietary changes to bowel preparation. But have you ever considered one of the most critical logistical details that often gets overlooked until the last minute? What happens once the procedure is over and it is time to head home? If you arrive for your colonoscopy without a designated driver to take you home, the medical facility will almost certainly cancel your procedure. It is a strict safety protocol that you simply cannot drive yourself, take public transportation alone, or use a standard taxi or ride share service without a companion after a colonoscopy. The reason for this strict rule lies with the sedation or anesthesia administered during the colonoscopy. While you may feel awake and alert shortly after the procedure, the medications remanges in your system. They impair your judgment, reflexes, and coordination for several hours, similar to the effects of alcohol. This impairment means you are not safe to operate a vehicle or make important decisions independently. So, what can you do if you realize you do not have a ride? The most important step is to plan ahead. Before your appointment, arrange for a trusted family member or friend to pick you up. If that is not possible, explore non-emergency medical transportation services in your area. Some clinics may also have a list of approved medical taxi services or specific ride share options that cater to post-procedure patient transport. It is not just about avoiding driving. These medications can also affect your short-term memory and ability to fully comprehend and remember crucial post-procedure instructions from your medical team. Having a responsible adult with you ensures you get home safely and that all important afterare details are clearly understood and followed leading to a smoother recovery. Ultimately, securing a reliable ride home is as vital to your safety and the success of your colonoscopy as the preparation itself. By arranging this detail in advance, you can approach your procedure with confidence, knowing you have covered all the necessary bases for a safe and comfortable return home and a full recovery. >> [music]

transcript_text: Proper bowel preparation is key to a successful colonoscopy. It allows your doctor to clearly view the colon lining and detect even small polyps. Preparation starts with a low residue diet 5 days before the procedure. This means avoiding hard-to-digest foods like nuts, seeds, raw fruits and vegetables, and whole grains. Instead, choose low-fiber options like white bread, rice, pasta, well-cooked or canned vegetables without skins, lean meats, eggs, and small amounts of dairy. The day before the procedure, you'll switch to a clear liquid diet. This includes water, apple juice, plain tea or coffee without milk, and electrolyte drinks. You'll also take a laxative solution, typically in two doses, one the evening before and one early the morning of the procedure. This triggers frequent bowel movements to fully empty the colon. title: ASL: Getting Ready for Your Colonoscopy
description:
Getting Ready for Your Colonoscopy

This video will guide you through the preparation for a colonoscopy procedure at
the University of Vermont Medical Center.

A colonoscopy is a procedure that is used to screen for colon cancer or other conditions of the large intestine.

Because there are many things you have to do starting 7 days before the procedure, please watch all the way to the end of this  video.  If you are unable to do all that is required, you may be turned away from your appointment. 

If you need assistance please call 802 847 8899 for an interpreter, and tell the receptionist the language that you need. 

Ask them to connect you to 802-847-8865 extension 2.  You will then be connected with the office and someone who can help you.  

Seven days before your colonoscopy, you will need to call your pharmacy to make sure there is a prescription for your preparation. 

You will need to get this prescription at least seven days before your scheduled procedure. Please contact the office if you are having difficulty with your prescription.

You will also need to arrange a ride home from the hospital. You must have a responsible adult drive you home or be responsible for you on public transportation. This person does not have to stay at the hospital while you have your procedure,

but must be within 15 minutes of the hospital. 

Your estimated time of stay is two hours from registration to discharge. 

You will need:  
Four Dulcolax laxative or generic bisacodyl laxative tablets
One 238 gram bottle of Miralax or generic polyethylene glycol
Sixty Four ounces of Gatorade that are not red or purple

Stop eating foods with seeds and nuts for the seven days before your procedure. This includes foods that have seeds or nuts on them: bagels, cucumbers, tomatoes, bread, popcorn. 

If you take blood thinning medication, diabetes medication, or medication for weight loss, please call your primary care provider to ask how you should take these medications before and after your colonoscopy.  

Stop taking iron and herbal supplements 7 days before your procedure.

One day before your colonoscopy, there are guidelines that must be followed to complete your preparation. 

You cannot eat food of any kind today except for popsicles that are not red or purple. 

You may have any of these liquids: water, apple juice, white grape juice, ginger ale, sports drinks like PowerAde or Gatorade that are not red or purple, Crystal Light, black coffee, black tea, Kool Aid that is not red or purple. 

You may not have any liquid that is red or purple, Jello, broth, juices with pulp, ice cream, alcohol, gum, any food, or anything that is not one of the liquids we just mentioned. 

Please take your approved medications today as prescribed by your doctor. Follow your instructions for diabetes medication, weight loss medication and blood thinners. 

NO herbal medications or Iron tablets.

Miralax Preparation Instructions:

At 5PM: Take four Dulcolax or generic bisacodyl pills with a full glass of water

At 6PM: Mix one 238-gram bottle of Miralax or generic polyethylene glycol and 64 ounces of Gatorade that is not red or purple into a big container. 

Drink one 8-ounce glass of the mixture every 15 minutes until you finish HALF of the container. 

Refrigerate the rest of the mixture in the container. 

You must finish half of it even if you have diarrhea. 

If you become nauseous, stop for 30 minutes and then start drinking again

until you are finished with the first half of the preparation.

 It may also help to drink through a straw. 

You may drink as much of the acceptable liquids along with the Miralax solution as you like including water. The more fluids you drink, the cleaner your colon will be. 

Use Desitin on your bottom if it is sore. 

On the day of your colonoscopy:

5 hours before your procedure, drink 8 ounces of the remaining mixture, every 15 minutes, until it is finished. You must finish all the preparation within two hours. 

You are not permitted to drink anything within the three hours before your procedure time. Drinking anything within the three hours may delay or cancel your procedure.

Your stool output should be clear yellow, like urine. If you are concerned that your stool is not clear in color 

please contact the office at 802-847-8865 extension 2.

title: Webinar: Inside the New ACS Colorectal Cancer Screening Guidelines
description: In this timely webinar session, Robert Smith, PhD, Senior Vice President of Cancer Screening, ACS, provided an in-depth overview of the newly updated American Cancer Society (ACS) colorectal cancer screening guidelines and the evidence supporting them, offering clarity on what these changes mean for screening and early detection. The session also featured a moderated Q&A with ACS NCCRT Vice Chair, Gloria Coronado, PhD, providing attendees the opportunity to engage directly on key questions.
channel_description: The ultimate goal of the ACS NCCRT is to increase the use of proven colorectal cancer screening tests among the entire population for whom screening is appropriate.

One in three people is overdue for colorectal cancer screening according to the American Cancer Society (2020). You have many screening test options including colonoscopy and at-home tests.
